title: What having bad genetics means (to me)
summary: He defines 'bad genetics' as a poor starting point, not a low ceiling: he was a 140 lb stick after puberty, so getting where he is took twice as long as someone gifted. He denies that any natural has maxed out their potential, describes the 'Schrodinger's bodybuilder' trap where critics call you small or genetically gifted depending on results, and urges people to start and keep working regardless of genetics.

claims.claim: For him bad genetics are defined by where you start, not where you end, because there is no end point.
No natural on the planet has maxed out their genetic limits; there is always a body part to focus on or something more to do.
Claiming you've maxed out your natural potential is arrogant; you're either lazy or unwilling to research further ways to progress.
Kids he knew at 13-14 had six packs and visible bicep veins without ever doing a push-up; that is what good genetics looks like: a better start.
He considers his genetics bad because at 18, past puberty and training a lot, he was still a 140 lb stick.
A person with good genetics could reach his current level in about half the time it took him.
'Schrodinger's bodybuilder': if he'd never trained, people would say he's small because he never tried; once he got big, they say it's because he had good genetics all along.
Critics always find a way to take your accomplishments away: either you had good genetics, or you're not actually that big.
Whatever your genetics, what matters is starting and doing the work; if you do nothing, genetics are irrelevant.
Genetics matter for things like injury prevention and some aspects of diet, but are irrelevant to reaching your potential because you have to work regardless.
Even if a stick could reveal your genetic level and it was low, sitting on the couch would make no sense.
Everyone told him he had bad genetics and was wasting his time; it didn't stop him. In five years you'll regret not starting now.
On his channel genetics won't be treated as an important factor for natural bodybuilding as long as you're willing to put in the work.
Giving up before even trying is worse than defeat; everyone can achieve the body they want to a certain extent.
